rejected.title: Views on sustainability
card: Acting on the environment has costs and benefits. Different groups weigh them differently, because the costs and benefits land on them in different ways.
Households
may gain from lower power bills or cleaner air, but face the up-front cost of items such as solar panels or an electric car.
Businesses
look at costs, profit and customers. Cutting emissions may raise costs, or it may save energy and win customers who want greener products.
Governments

weigh the needs of the wider community, such as jobs, public health and budget costs. Groups tied to one industry, such as miners or farmers, may see a different balance again, as their income can depend on how the rules change.
rejected.remember: People differ on sustainability because the costs and benefits of acting fall on them differently.

a.q: Why might a coal miner and a household with solar panels hold different views on cutting emissions?
opts: The costs and benefits of acting fall on each differently
Miners understand climate science less well than households
The household's income depends more on coal than the miner's
Governments decide what each group thinks about emissions
a.why: A miner's income may depend on coal, while a household with solar panels may save on power bills. Each weighs a different set of costs and benefits. The option about miners understanding climate science less well is tempting, but the card explains the difference through who gains and who pays, not through what each group knows.
a.clue: Think about who gains and who loses in each case.

b.q: Priya runs a bakery in Ballarat. Gas ovens are cheap to run, and new electric ovens cost a lot up front. Which reason best explains why she might delay switching?
opts: The up-front cost may outweigh the gains to her business
Greener ovens may win her customers who want them
Businesses may leave choices about ovens to governments
Cutting emissions may lower her bakery's costs right away
b.why: A business weighs costs against its own benefits, and a large up-front cost can outweigh them for now. The option about greener ovens winning customers is tempting because the card mentions it, but it is a benefit of switching, so it is a reason to switch rather than to delay.
b.clue: Which reason points towards waiting, not switching?

a.q: Why might a coal miner and a household with solar panels hold different views on cutting emissions?
opts: The costs and benefits of acting fall on each differently
Miners have no interest in the environment at all
Households face no costs when they cut emissions
Only governments are affected by emissions policies
a.why: A miner's income may depend on coal, while a household may save on power bills. Each weighs different costs and benefits. It is not true that miners have no interest in the environment, as the card only says their balance of costs and benefits can differ.
a.clue: Think about who gains and who loses in each case.

b.q: Priya runs a bakery in Ballarat. Gas ovens are cheap to run, and new electric ovens cost a lot up front. Which reason best explains why she might delay switching?
opts: The up-front cost may outweigh the gains to her business
Businesses are not affected by cutting emissions at all
Switching ovens is a choice that only governments make
Greener ovens could not win her any extra customers
b.why: A business weighs costs against its own benefits, and a large up-front cost can outweigh them for now. The last option is tempting, but the card says some customers may want greener products, so it is not a sound reason.
b.clue: Look at what the business pays and gains itself.
